A 70-year-old man arrives at the emergency department with sudden onset of shortness of breath that
began while he was working on his car at home. He had been exposed to various chemicals and
inhalants while repairing the engine. His symptoms did not improve with rest, and paramedics
transported him to the hospital, where he is now receiving 100% oxygen via nasal cannula. The patient
has a 52-pack-year smoking history, drinks 2–3 alcoholic beverages nightly, and has a history of
asthma but has not seen a physician since high school. His vital signs are as follows: temperature
97.8°F (36.8°C), blood pressure 142/107 mmHg, pulse 102/min, respirations 21/min, and oxygen
saturation 77%. Physical examination reveals tachycardia with a systolic murmur best heard at the
right upper sternal border, diminished breath sounds over the right upper lobe, and bilateral lower
extremity pitting edema. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? Answer Choices: (A) Acute
right heart failure (B) Rupture of an emphysematous bleb (C) Tension pneumothorax (D) Chemical
pneumonitis from inhaled toxins (E) Methemoglobinemia from chemical exposure (F) Acute
exacerbation of underlying COPD (G) Right-sided pulmonary embolism (H) Bronchial obstruction from
mucus plugging (I) Pulmonary edema secondary to decreased cardiac output (J) Fe3+ hemoglobin in

circulating red blood cells
 A. Bronchial obstruction from mucus plugging
B. Methemoglobinemia from chemical exposure
C. Fe3+ hemoglobin in circulating red blood cells
D. Chemical pneumonitis from inhaled toxins
E. Acute right heart failure
F. Rupture of an emphysematous bleb
G. Pulmonary edema secondary to decreased cardiac output
H. Right-sided pulmonary embolism
I. Tension pneumothorax
J. Acute exacerbation of underlying COPD
